title: Bishop and knight I: the W manoeuvre
summary: From the wrong corner to the right one, with the knight drawing a W.
step.corner: This is the mate that embarrasses masters the most. De la Villa tells of players who went home with their heads down for not knowing it. Look at the position: the black king is already on the edge, huddled in h8. It looks almost over, but h8 is a dark square and your bishop only walks on light ones. That is the wrong corner. The mate only exists in the corner of the bishop's colour: a8 or h1. Our journey is to take the king from h8 to a8, along the eighth rank.
step.whyWrong: Why does the corner matter? Look at the finished mate in the right corner. The black king on a8, a light square. Your king on b6 takes a7 and b7, the knight on a6 takes b8, and the bishop gives check along the long diagonal. Everything fits. In the dark corner the bishop reaches neither the king nor the corner square, and too much is left for the knight. The tablebase confirms it: from there the mate cannot be forced. So we empty the wrong corner and close the right one.
step.wShape: Now the secret, which Philidor already pointed out in 1777: the knight's path. On the eighth rank the dark squares are h8, f8, d8 and b8, and those are the ones the black king needs. The knight will take them one by one: f7, e5, d7, c5, b7. Draw it on the board and you will see a W. Each point of the W takes a dark square; the bishop does the rest on the light ones. Let us play this W together, move by move.
step.w1: First point of the W. The king is on h8 and your knight on e5. Take h8 from him, with check.
step.w1.hint: The knight from e5 gives check on the square that also covers h8. Look on the seventh rank.
step.w1.done: Nf7+. The king has only g8, and h8 is gone for good. First point done.
step.w2: The king went to g8 and wants to come back. The next square to take is g8, a light one: the bishop's job. But it cannot get there in one move. First prepare the bishop on the diagonal, then bring it to h7, and when the king steps onto e8, bring the knight back to the centre, on e5. Three moves of yours.
step.w2.hint: Bishop onto the b1–h7 diagonal first: from f5 it reaches h7. After Bh7 the king goes to e8 and the knight returns to e5, where it covers d7.
step.w2.done: Bf5, Bh7 and Ne5. The king has lost g8 and f8 and stands on e8, and the knight already covers d7, the door to the centre. Second point of the W.
step.w3: The black king stepped onto d8 and will try to escape along the seventh rank: c7, then b6 or c5. First bring your king to e6, to take d7 and e7. When he goes to c7, the third point of the W, on d7, takes b6 and c5 from him.
step.w3.hint: King to e6 first. After the black king reaches c7, the knight jumps from e5 to d7 and covers b6 and c5.
step.w3.done: Ke6 and Nd7. The king ran to b7, but look at what he has: b6 and c5 belong to the knight, c7 and d7 to you. Third point.
step.w4: The black king is on b7 and looks at c6, from where he wants to reach b5 and c4. Before he gets out, close both squares with the bishop, in one move.
step.w4.hint: One square on the b1–h7 diagonal covers b5 and c4 at the same time. The bishop goes back the way it came.
step.w4.done: Bd3. Now the black king goes to c6 and stops: b5 and c4 belong to the bishop, b6, c5 and d7 to the knight and your king. The net is closed.
step.w5: The black king is on c6 with no way out. You need to pass the move to him without letting anything go. The bishop does that: a waiting move along the diagonal, and on the next move it takes the long diagonal, a8–h1, its home until the mate.
step.w5.hint: Bishop to e2, waiting; the black king returns to c7. Then bishop to f3, on the long diagonal.
step.w5.done: Be2 and Bf3. The black king can no longer stay on the seventh and goes back to the eighth. Notice: the bishop on f3 covers b7, the square where the black king would love to sit.
step.w6: Now the final push along the eighth. The black king is on d8. Take d6 with your king; he goes to e8, trying the far side. Chase him off with a bishop check on h5, and bring the bishop to f7, where it covers e8 and g8. Then the knight makes the last two points of the W: c5 and b7 with check. Five moves of yours.
step.w6.hint: Kd6, then Bh5+ and Bf7. With the bishop on f7, the knight goes from d7 to c5 and from c5 to b7 with check.
step.w6.done: Kd6, Bh5+, Bf7, Nc5 and Nb7+. The W is complete: f7, e5, d7, c5, b7. The black king is stuck on c8 and can only go to b8. Only the mate is left.
step.escape: Go back a little. After Bh7 and Ke8, not every king goes to d8. Some try to return to the wrong corner: Kf8, eyeing g8 and h8. Karttunen beat Rasik that way in 2003, punishing every retreat. Punish this one: knight check, and the white king takes e6.
step.escape.hint: The knight from e5 gives check on d7 and at the same time covers f8. After Ke8, your king goes to e6.
step.escape.done: Nd7+ and Ke6. The black king lost f8 and g8 at once, and your king is already on e6. Going back to the wrong corner only shortens his road.
step.trap: Near the right corner lives a trap, found by Frederick Rhine in 2000. White to play, and Nb6+ looks natural: check, and the king goes to b7, doesn't it? No. The king goes to d8 and attacks the bishop on e8. Now every bishop move leaves the black king without a move: stalemate. And any other move loses the bishop, and king and knight cannot mate. Draw. Rule: near the corner, before every knight check, see whether the bishop is safe and whether the black king still has a square.
step.finish: The W is done. The black king is on c8, the knight on b7, the bishop on f7. Now the mate: bring your king to c6 and b6, give a bishop check on e6 when the black king is on c8, bring the knight to c5, wait with the bishop on d7, and close with Na6+ and Bc6. Seven moves, and no stalemate on the way.
step.finish.hint: Kc6 and Kb6 first. The black king on c8 gets Be6+. Then Nc5, a waiting Bd7, Na6+ and the mate with the bishop on c6.
step.finish.done: Checkmate. King on b6, knight on a6, bishop on c6: the pattern we saw at the start. You took the king from the wrong corner to the right one and shut the door.
step.rules: Three rules to take into your games. First: the mate is in the corner of the bishop's colour; if the king is in the other one, the journey goes along the edge. Second: the knight takes the dark squares of the edge in a W: f7, e5, d7, c5, b7; the bishop takes the light ones and gives the final check. Third: near the corner, before every knight check, check for stalemate and for the bishop. Now you play.
step.playW: The whole W position. The black king on h8, the wrong corner. Take him to a8 and mate. No hurry: the fifty-move rule is generous to those who know the way.
step.playFar: A little further out. The knight is still on d3 and the black king on g8. Build the W first: knight to e5, king to f6, knight to f7. Then the road you already know.
ex.e01: White to play and mate. The black king is on a8, the right corner. Only the bishop's move is missing.
ex.e01.hint: The king on b6 and the knight on a6 have already taken every square from the black king. Only the bishop can give check, and only along the long diagonal.
ex.e01.solution: Bg2 is mate: the check comes along the a8–h1 diagonal, b8 belongs to the knight, a7 and b7 to the king. Note that any other bishop move would stalemate the black king: he had no square at all.
ex.e02: White to play and win. The black king is on b8. Two moves of yours to mate.
ex.e02.hint: Take b8 with a knight check: the black king will have only a8. Then the bishop closes the long diagonal.
ex.e02.solution: Na6+ forces Ka8 (c8 belongs to the bishop, a7 and b7 to the king), and Bc6 mates along the long diagonal. It is the final pattern of the W.
ex.e03: White to play and win. The black king has just gone to g8. The knight on f7 already takes h8. What is the next step?
ex.e03.hint: The next square to take is g8, a light one. The bishop will cover it from h7, but first it has to reach the right diagonal.
ex.e03.solution: Bf5 (or another square on the b1–h7 diagonal, such as Be4 or Bg6). The black king is forced to f8, and Bh7 takes g8 from him. The bishop always needs one preparatory move here.
ex.e04: White to play and win. The key position of the lesson: black king on h8, the wrong corner. Start the W.
ex.e04.hint: The black king has only one square. Take h8 from him right away, with the knight.
ex.e04.solution: Nf7+, the first point of the W: the king goes to g8 and never returns to h8. A waiting move with the bishop on the b1–h7 diagonal (or Ng6+) works too, because the black king has to leave anyway; but the W starts with the knight on f7.
ex.e05: White to play and win. The black king has reached e8 and wants to leave the edge via d7. Stop him.
ex.e05.hint: The square d7 is dark: the knight's job. From where does it cover d7 and still stay on the path of the W?
ex.e05.solution: Ne5, the second point of the W. The knight covers d7 and f7, and the black king has to choose between d8 and f8. Any other move let the king out to d7 and delayed the mate a great deal.
ex.e06: White to play and win. The black king is on a8 and you are close to mate. But careful: the move that looks obvious is a draw. Three moves of yours.
ex.e06.hint: Na6 now takes the black king's last square without check: stalemate. Move the bishop to a square from which it reaches the long diagonal at the right moment.
ex.e06.solution: Bg4 (or Be2) leaves b8 to the black king. After Kb8, Na6+ forces Ka8 and Bf3 mates along the long diagonal. The bishop waited one step from the diagonal and only entered it when the check was mate.
ex.e07: White to play and win. Rhine's trap: the knight check on b6 looks winning. Find a move that does not draw.
ex.e07.hint: After Nb6+ Kd8 the bishop on e8 is trapped, and every bishop move stalemates. Before any check, take the bishop out of the black king's reach, or bring the knight another way.
ex.e07.solution: Bb5 (or Ba4, Bc6, Na5, Ke7) keeps the black king locked in the corner and the bishop safe. One road: Bb5 Kd8, Na5 Kc8, Bd7+ Kb8, Kc6 Ka7, Bc8 Kb8, Kd7 Ka7, Kc7 Ka8, Bb7+ Ka7, Nc6 mate. What fails is Nb6+?? Kd8!, which draws.
ex.e08: White to play and win. The black king escaped to b7 and looks at c6, b5 and c4. Close the net.
ex.e08.hint: Two light squares need an owner: b5 and c4. One square on the b1–h7 diagonal covers both.
ex.e08.solution: Bd3 covers b5 and c4. The black king goes to c6 and gets no further: b6, c5 and d7 belong to the knight and your king. Bringing the king closer via d5 or d6 also wins, but the bishop closes the net more clearly.
ex.e09: White to play and win. Now the bishop is a dark-squared one and the black king is on h1, a light corner. The wrong corner again, only at the bottom. Start the W.
ex.e09.hint: The W is the same, turned over. The knight from e4 gives check on the square that also covers h1.
ex.e09.solution: Nf2+, the first point of the lower W: f2, e4, d2, c4, b2. The black king goes to g1 and the mate will be on a1, the dark corner, your bishop's home. As in the upper corner, a waiting bishop move also works, but the W starts with the knight.
ex.e10: White to play and win. The black king went back to e8 after Nd7+. Three moves of yours to push him towards the right corner.
ex.e10.hint: King to e6 and to d6, taking the seventh rank. When the black king goes to e8, a bishop check sends him back to d8.
ex.e10.solution: Ke6 Kd8, Kd6 Ke8, Bg6+ (or Bg8): the black king is forced to d8 and loses e8 for good. From there the knight goes to c5 and the mate follows as in the lesson.
ex.e11: White to play and win. The black king is on h8, but your pieces have not formed the W yet: the knight is on d3 and the bishop on e4. Build the key position in three moves.
ex.e11.hint: Knight to the centre, on e5; then the first point of the W, on f7; and when the king goes to f8, the bishop takes g8 from h7.
ex.e11.solution: Ne5 Kg8, Nf7 Kf8, Bh7: the W position with g8 already taken, because the bishop was ready on the b1–h7 diagonal. The black king goes to e8 and the lesson's road continues with Ne5.
ex.e12: White to play and win. The mirrored W: dark-squared bishop, black king on b8 after the first check, and the mate will be on h8. Three moves of yours.
ex.e12.hint: It is the same idea as Bf5, Bh7 and Ne5, mirrored: the bishop prepares and takes b8 from a7, and the knight returns to the centre to cover e7.
ex.e12.solution: Bc5 (or another square on the a7–g1 diagonal) Kc8, Ba7 Kd8, Nd5: the black king has lost c8 and b8 and the knight covers e7. From there the W runs along the eighth rank to h8.
key.wStart: The key position of the W: black king on h8, the wrong corner. The whole line, credited to Müller and Lamprecht, is in the Wikipedia article on the mate.
key.mateCorner: The mating pattern in the right corner: king on b6, knight on a6, bishop on c6. The same Müller and Lamprecht pattern the lesson teaches you to reach.
key.rhineTrap: Rhine's trap (2000): Nb6+?? Kd8! and the bishop is trapped. Every bishop move stalemates; anything else loses the bishop.
key.escapeBack: The retreat to the wrong corner (4...Kf8) and its punishment: Nd7+. A lesson position, taken from the W line.
key.stalemateAlert: The stalemate alert: Na6?? leaves the black king without a move. The bishop waits one step from the long diagonal.
history: Philidor, in 1777, was the first to describe the knight's path we now call the W. In 1923 the Frenchman Daniel Delétang published another method, the triangles, which the Lichess practice section teaches to this day. The mate is rare: Müller and Lamprecht count one in every six thousand games. That is why Silman left it out of his endgame course, and Soltis answers that learning it teaches piece coordination like nothing else. In 1997 Tal Shaked beat Morozevich with this mate in the penultimate round of the World Junior Championship and took the title. In 2003 Karttunen beat Rasik with the knight's W. And grandmasters have failed: Epishin stalemated Kempinski's king in 2001, and Anna Ushenina, world champion, could not deliver the mate against Olga Girya in Geneva, 2013.
practice: Now the real endgame. In this position the black king is near h1, the right corner for your bishop: close the net and mate without stalemating. Pick a pace and challenge the clock, or set up your own training.
